source_text:
Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἅμα τῷ τεχθῆναι τὰ παιδία, τελείας ἐξῆπτο φρονήσεως, ἐξῆν ἴσως ὑποκρίνεσθαί τινας ἄνοιαν· εἰ δὲ λείπεται νοῦ καὶ λόγου καὶ
συνέσεως, οὐκ ἄρα καθέστηκαν ἀγέννητοι τὴν φύσιν αἱ ψυχαί. Σύμπαντες οὖν ἴσμεν, ὅτι τοῖς τῶν σωμάτων ὄγκοις ἡ ψυχὴ συνεκτέταται, διαρκῶς οὐ μεγέθει μόνον ἢ βραχύτητι μελῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταῖς ἄλλαις τῆς γνώμης ἀλογίαις· ἐς ὅσον μὲν νεόπλαστα τυγχάνει ταῦτα τὰ βρέφη, πάσης μὲν πανταχῶς ἐννοίας ἀπορεῖ καὶ βουλῆς· ἡρέμα δὲ καὶ κατ' ὀλίγον προϊόντα νοῦν τε καὶ φρόνησιν προσλαμβάνει καὶ λόγον.
thought_title: Infants lack mind, so souls are not unbegotten
orientation: Eustathius is addressing the Pythagoreans and Platonists, arguing from the observable condition of newborn infants that souls are not unbegotten.
pass_a_gloss: For if at the same time as being born the children had been attached to complete wisdom, it would perhaps be possible for some to feign folly; but if they are lacking in mind and reason and understanding, then souls have not been established as unbegotten in nature. Therefore we all know that the soul has been stretched out together with the masses of bodies, enduringly not only in size or smallness of limbs, but also in the other irrationalities of the disposition; as long as these infants happen to be newly formed, it is at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel; but gently and little by little as they advance they take on in addition mind and wisdom and reason.

lemmas.gloss: has been stretched out together with

choices.english: had been attached to complete wisdom
choices.why: Keeps the pluperfect passive force of ἐξῆπτο (had been fastened/attached) and the genitive of the thing attached to, preserving the metaphor of connection rather than possession.
ὑποκρίνομαι means to pretend or play a part; 'feign' captures the theatrical sense and the accusative object ἄνοιαν.

choices.term: οὐκ ἄρα καθέστηκαν ἀγέννητοι τὴν φύσιν αἱ ψυχαί
choices.english: then souls have not been established as unbegotten in nature
choices.why: καθέστηκαν is perfect of καθίστημι, 'have been established/constituted'; the accusative τὴν φύσιν is a respect accusative rendered 'in nature'; ἀγέννητοι uses the glossary term 'unbegotten'.
rejected: souls are not unbegotten by nature
souls have not become unbegotten in nature

choices.english: has been stretched out together with
choices.why: The verb συνεκτείνω means to stretch out together with; the perfect passive conveys a state resulting from co-extension with the body's masses.

choices.english: in the other irrationalities of the disposition
choices.why: γνώμη here means the mind's disposition or judgment; ἀλογία is the privation of λόγος, rendered 'irrationalities' to keep the link with 'reason'.
rejected: in the other irrationalities of the mind
in the other unreasonablenesses of the judgment

choices.term: πάσης μὲν πανταχῶς ἐννοίας ἀπορεῖ καὶ βουλῆς
choices.english: it is at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel
choices.why: ἀπορέω with genitive means to be at a loss for/lack; πανταχῶς is adverbial 'everywhere/in every way', kept literally to preserve the emphatic universality.
rejected: it lacks all thought and counsel entirely
it is devoid of every notion and plan

pass_b_english: For if children at the very moment of birth had been attached to complete wisdom, it would perhaps be possible for some to feign folly. But if they are lacking in mind and reason and understanding, then souls have not been established as unbegotten in nature. We all know, then, that the soul has been stretched out together with the masses of the body—not only in the size or smallness of its limbs, but also in the other irrationalities of the disposition. As long as these infants are newly formed, these infants are at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel. But as they advance little by little and gradually, it takes on mind and wisdom and reason in addition.

problems.quote: the soul is at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel
problems.source_quote: πάσης μὲν πανταχῶς ἐννοίας ἀπορεῖ καὶ βουλῆς
problems.why: Subject is 'βρέφη' (infants), not 'soul'; English wrongly makes soul the subject.
problems.fix: these infants are at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel
problems.ruling: ἀπορεῖ subject is ταῦτα τὰ βρέφη (infants), not ψυχή; English wrongly inserts 'soul' as subject.

edits.old: the soul is at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel
edits.new: these infants are at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel

fixed: Changed the subject of the clause from 'the soul' to 'these infants' to match the Greek subject βρέφη.

problems.quote: the soul has been stretched out together with the masses of the body
problems.why: 'Stretched out' and 'masses' are awkward; suggests growth but is unidiomatic.
problems.fix: 'the soul develops together with the bulk of the body'

problems.quote: these infants are at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel
problems.why: 'Everywhere' is misplaced or redundant; 'for counsel' is abrupt.
problems.fix: 'these infants completely lack all thought and understanding'

problems.quote: it takes on mind and wisdom and reason in addition
problems.why: 'In addition' is vague—addition to what? Soul was previously without these.
problems.fix: 'it gradually acquires mind, wisdom, and reason'

edits.old: the soul has been stretched out together with the masses of the body
edits.new: the soul develops together with the bulk of the body

edits.old: these infants are at a loss for every thought everywhere and for counsel
edits.new: these infants completely lack all thought and counsel

edits.old: it takes on mind and wisdom and reason in addition
edits.new: it gradually acquires mind, wisdom, and reason

fixed: The first problem is real: 'stretched out together with the masses' is awkward and unidiomatic. Replaced with 'develops together with the bulk'.
The second problem is real: 'everywhere' is redundant and 'for counsel' is abrupt. Replaced with 'completely lack all thought and counsel'.
The third problem is real: 'in addition' is vague. Replaced with 'gradually acquires'.

last_rejected.quote: the other irrationalities of the disposition
last_rejected.why: ἀλογίαι here means 'deficiencies' or 'irrational states' of the soul's faculty, not 'irrationalities'; the point is the soul tracks bodily defects.
last_rejected.fix: the other deficiencies of the disposition
last_rejected.ruling: ἀλογίαι means 'irrationalities/lack of reason'; 'disposition' for γνώμης is standard; meaning preserved.

last_rejected.why: Glossary fixes 'understanding' as banned for νοῦς, not συνέσεως; but συνέσεως is not in glossary. However 'understanding' is banned for νοῦς, and the source has νοῦ καὶ λόγου καὶ συνέσεως. The English uses 'understanding' for συνέσεως, which is not banned. Wait—let me recheck: the banned term is for νοῦς specifically. Actually this is fine. Let me re-examine.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter self-corrects: 'understanding' for συνέσεως is not banned; no glossary violation exists.

last_rejected.quote: it takes on mind and wisdom and reason in addition
last_rejected.source_quote: νοῦν τε καὶ φρόνησιν προσλαμβάνει καὶ λόγον
last_rejected.why: Subject 'it' is unclear (soul or infant?); source says infants acquire these powers; 'in addition' is not in source.
last_rejected.fix: they gradually acquire mind and wisdom and reason
last_rejected.ruling: Subject 'it' refers to preceding infant(s); προσλαμβάνει naturally implies acquiring 'in addition'; meaning preserved.

last_rejected.quote: these infants are at a loss
last_rejected.source_quote: ἡρέμα δὲ καὶ κατ' ὀλίγον προϊόντα
last_rejected.why: English omits 'gently'/'gradually' (ἡρέμα) in the second clause, keeping only 'little by little'; ἡρέμα means gently/quietly/gradually.
last_rejected.fix: gently and little by little as they advance
last_rejected.ruling: ἡρέμα and κατ' ὀλίγον both convey gradualness; 'gradually' in next clause covers both; no meaning lost.
